rules.statement: When a method has generic and non-generic overloads with the same logic, implement the non-generic one by delegating to the generic one (with a wrapper returning a dummy value) instead of repeating the steps.
rules.why: Duplicated logic has to be changed twice, and the copies can drift.
rules.check: Look for paired generic/non-generic overloads whose bodies repeat the same sequence of steps.

rules.statement: When several parameters are shared state that always travel together through a method, group them into a small state type, or make the method a member of a class that holds that state.
rules.why: Long signatures are hard to read and grow with every new piece of shared state.
rules.check: Look for methods taking many parameters (around seven plus a token) where a subset is the same shared state passed together at every call.

rules.statement: Don't ask to group parameters into a descriptor type when they are separate facts about a call, or when they mirror the fields of an existing record that the method builds or fills.
rules.why: The record already groups them, so a new descriptor would duplicate it and be built at every call site only to carry the same values.
rules.check: Before reporting a long parameter list, check whether the parameters map onto an existing record's constructor or are distinct facts the method passes on.

rules.statement: Don't report a bool parameter as a mode flag when it carries data, such as a declared guarantee or capability that the method checks against.
rules.why: The conventions allow a bool carried as data. Only bools that switch between behaviours are a smell.
rules.check: Before reporting, see whether the bool's value comes from data (a declared capability or a property read by the caller) and whether sibling methods take it the same way.

rules.statement: Don't ask to pass a composite value instead of separate parameters when the parameters are computed once outside a loop and passing the composite would recompute them on every iteration.
rules.why: The separate parameters exist to avoid repeating work, such as decoding, inside the scan.
rules.check: Check whether the separate arguments are hoisted computations reused across a loop that calls the method.

rules.statement: Don't report as nested calls that should be hoisted: a `with` initializer's values, a `new` expression passed as an argument, `TimeSpan.From*` of a literal, or a chain of calls on one receiver.
rules.why: A `with` initializer isn't a call's argument, and these forms are deliberately kept inline. The hoisting rule targets calls nested in other calls' arguments, such as in string interpolations.
rules.check: Before reporting a nested call, check whether it is one of these allowed inline forms.

rules.statement: When a method dispatches many operations in one long switch, put each operation's handling in its own private helper so the switch only dispatches.
rules.why: A single long switch is harder to follow and extend than per-operation helpers.
rules.check: Look for long switch statements whose branches contain the full logic for each operation, unlike sibling types that already split it.

rules.statement: Don't ask to extract each rule of a single-pass check into its own helper when the rules share that pass's state and each helper would need four or more parameters.
rules.why: Splitting would break the few-parameters rule. When each rule already has its own test, splitting adds nothing.
rules.check: Before reporting, see whether the rules in a long loop share mutable loop state and are already tested one by one.

rules.statement: Don't ask to replace `new` of a positional record with a `with` expression when the branch states the whole next state and keeps only one or two members.
rules.why: Adding a member to a positional record changes its constructor, so every `new` stops compiling instead of silently resetting the member, and no convention asks for `with` here.
rules.check: Check that the record is positional and that the branch sets most members anew, rather than changing one or two.

rules.statement: Document every `ArgumentNullException` a public method throws (for example from `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull`) with an `<exception cref="ArgumentNullException">` tag.
rules.why: Otherwise the docs don't say that null arguments throw.
rules.check: Look for public methods calling `ThrowIfNull` or throwing `ArgumentNullException` without a matching `<exception>` doc tag.

rules.statement: Don't report a nested scan (deliveries × history) in test-only checking code as a performance problem when the run sizes are small and fixed by the test harness.
rules.why: The cost is not measurable at those sizes, and an index would add a second structure that must keep the scan's rules in sync.
rules.check: Check the harness's fixed run sizes (clients, steps, keys) before reporting a quadratic scan in test tooling.

rules.statement: Don't ask to speed up a failure-shrinking search (such as finding the shortest failing prefix) when it only runs for a test that is already failing and its steps are bounded.
rules.why: Only failing tests pay the cost. A shortcut such as falling back to the full history would drop the shortest failing prefix that the design promises in the report.
rules.check: Check whether the code path runs only after a failure has been decided, and whether a design record promises its output.

rules.statement: When a test records an expected call and also runs the real call with the same values, declare those values once as named locals or constants and use them in both places.
rules.why: If the copies drift, the model is checked against a call the provider never ran.
rules.check: Look for the same bare literals repeated in an expected or recorded call and in the real call next to it.

rules.statement: Don't report a test helper for taking `params IEnumerable<T>`. The maintainer's C# conventions prefer it to `params T[]`, with buffering inside, and `IReadOnlyList<T>` is meant for a list parameter that isn't `params`.
rules.why: No convention keeps `params` out of test helpers.
rules.check: Before reporting, check whether the parameter is `params` and whether the helper buffers the enumerable inside.

rules.statement: Wrap XML doc comment lines at about 120 columns.
rules.why: Overlong lines are hard to read and need reflowing later.
rules.check: Look for `///` lines much longer than 120 columns.

rules.statement: Don't ask a test project to add a fault test for each method of a forwarding decorator when each forward is one call through a shared path whose faults are already tested, and contract tests run every forward.
rules.why: A drop test per method would repeat what the shared-path tests and the contract tests already show.
rules.check: Check whether each decorator method only forwards through one shared, tested wrapper, and whether a contract suite covers all the forwards.

rules.statement: Don't ask a test helper that mirrors a record's positional constructor to group its parameters into a new type.
rules.why: A test that builds the record states each of its fields. A grouping type would exist only for tests, beside a record that already names those fields.
rules.check: Check whether the helper's parameters match an existing record's constructor fields.

rules.statement: Don't suggest a per-caller context type for recording helpers when every call site would have to build it just to carry the same two values.
rules.why: The values are separate facts: one shared history and the caller of one call, which the caller gets per call. A context type would only add construction at every call site.
rules.check: Check where the repeated parameters come from at each call site, and whether they vary per call.
